messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Crowding: Crowded places, Moral Violation: People misbehaving
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Taufa is a 53-year-old Tongan-American airline pilot who has been married for twenty-six years and has, by most external measures, built a life of considerable stability and accomplishment. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 70, referred through his airline's employee assistance programme after a colleague noticed him gripping a cockpit door handle for nearly a full minute before he could bring himself to let go of it.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rangi was travelling on a layover in a country he has asked not to be named in his file. He was detained without explanation at a checkpoint, taken to a facility he could not identify, and held for eleven days. During that time he was subjected to systematic torture. He was kept in a cell that was intermittently plunged into total silence — no ventilation sound, no voices, nothing — and he came to understand, through repetition, that the silence meant someone was about to come through the door. The door itself was thick and industrial, with a heavy bolt that he could hear sliding before every session. The smell in the room was a specific compound of mildew, chemical disinfectant, and something metallic he has never been able to name precisely. On two occasions another detainee in an adjacent cell wept loudly and uncontrollably, and both times what followed for Rangi was among the worst of what he experienced. He was eventually released without charge and repatriated. He told his wife he had been in an accident. He told his employer he had been ill.

In the months that followed, Rangi continued flying. The professional structure of the cockpit — its checklists, its clear hierarchies, its noise — initially felt like the one place he could function. But the job also placed him in proximity to the very things that had become unbearable. Crowded boarding gates, which he must pass through on every trip, produce in him a vigilance so acute that he finds himself scanning faces methodically, reading posture, watching hands, certain that somewhere in the press of bodies there is a person who intends him harm. He has begun arriving at gates late, after most passengers have boarded, and his punctuality record — once impeccable — has attracted comment from his chief pilot.

At home, he checks the locks on every door and window before he can sleep, and again when he wakes in the night. His wife, Mele, initially interpreted this as a quirk that would pass. It has not passed. He cannot explain to her, or fully to himself, why the possibility of an unlocked door feels less like a risk and more like a certainty of catastrophe. When the house goes quiet — when the refrigerator hum drops out or the street outside stills — he is immediately and completely elsewhere, his body convinced that something is about to enter.

When Rangi attempts to recall what happened to him in any deliberate way, the memory does not arrive as a narrative. It arrives as a series of still images, precise and flat, like photographs laid out on a table — the bolt on the door, the particular angle of a fluorescent light, a man's shoes. Alongside those images comes the smell, immediate and specific, and when it arrives he cannot locate himself in his kitchen or his office or his cockpit. He has learned to stop the attempt quickly, because if he does not, the emotion that follows is of a magnitude he cannot manage in any setting where he is visible to others. He has not told Mele what the images contain.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the door handle incident, though that frightened him. It was a moment three weeks ago in the crew lounge when a junior flight attendant began crying after a difficult passenger interaction, and Rangi had to leave the room and sit alone in a stairwell for forty minutes before he could return to work. He had come to believe he was managing. That afternoon made clear to him that he was not. What he fears most, sitting in the intake room, is that he will be grounded. What he hopes for, though he has not yet said this aloud, is that someone will tell him it is possible to stop waiting for the door.
